napping-nsdr-yoga-nidra.text: Users nap or do NSDR and yoga nidra to make up for lost sleep and lower stress, aiming for a rested, less drawn look. Naps have been studied for alertness and performance; yoga nidra has small studies on relaxation, and none look at appearance.

deload-weeks-rest-days.text: Lifters schedule deloads and rest days so fatigue dissipates and training can continue progressing toward a more muscular physique. The approach rests on periodization theory; direct trials of deloads are sparse and none measure appearance.

massage-foam-rolling-recovery-gear.text: Foam rollers and massage tools are used to ease soreness and loosen tight muscles so users can train more often and move better, with a view to physique and posture. Studies report some short-term mobility and soreness benefits; appearance outcomes are not studied.

chain: Less cognitive hit from poor sleep
creatine-for-sleep-deprivation.text: Fitness and looksmaxxing posters take creatine to cushion the mental slump after short nights, so training and routines stay on track for physique goals. Small studies have examined cognition under sleep loss; none address how sleep-deprived people look.

sleep-banking.text: People sleep extra ahead of a planned short-sleep stretch, such as travel or a heavy schedule, hoping to stay sharp and look rested. It has been studied in military and shift-work settings with unsettled results, and not for appearance.

sleep-to-look-attractive-beauty-sleep-re.text: Appearance communities treat enough sleep as a baseline for a fresher face, citing research in which sleep-deprived faces were rated as less healthy and less attractive. Visible signs of sleep loss such as puffy eyes, paler skin and droopy lids are documented in studies.

eight-hours-target-sleep-is-looksmaxxing.text: 'Sleep is looksmaxxing' is a community slogan treating regular sleep, often about eight hours, as the foundation for skin, recovery and body composition. Adult sleep guidance recommends 7 to 9 hours, and sleep loss has documented visible effects on the face.

keto-ketogenic-diet.text: Some users follow keto to lean out and, in anecdotal accounts, to calm acne. It is established as a therapy for epilepsy, has mixed results for weight loss, and has not been tested for skin in the sources here.

chain: Lower calorie intake, less water weight
low-carb-diet.text: Users cut carbohydrates to lose fat and sharpen their physique, and some pair it with high protein to keep muscle while cutting. Trials show slightly faster early weight loss than low-fat diets, with the gap narrowing over time.

beef-salt-and-water-diet.text: Followers of the lion diet eat only ruminant meat, salt and water, promoting it for leanness, clearer skin and mood. It rests on testimonials; no controlled studies of this diet exist.

zero-carb-carnivore.text: Adherents eat only animal products to lose fat, hold muscle and, they say, clear skin and inflammation. Support comes mostly from self-reports, and dietetic bodies classify it as a fad diet.

ribeye-and-water-carnivore.text: Followers narrow carnivore eating to fatty beef and water, aiming for leanness, muscle and clearer skin through simplicity. It is an informal shorthand with no studies of its own.

chain: Clearer skin, leaner, more energy claimed
carnivore-ish-animal-based-diet.text: Popularised by Paul Saladino, this looser carnivore diet is followed for clearer skin, better sleep and energy, and a leaner physique. Evidence is mostly testimonials; controlled research is limited.

raw-egg-consumption.text: Raw eggs are blended into shakes in strength-sports culture as an inexpensive protein and choline source for building muscle. Research reports lower protein absorption from raw than cooked eggs, and no appearance studies exist.

chain: Vitamin A, B12 and iron intake
liver-organ-meats-beef-liver.text: Forum users eat beef liver as a nutrient-dense food for skin and vitality, citing its vitamin A, B12 and iron content. The nutrient content is well documented; trials on appearance have not been done.

desiccated-organ-supplements-beef-organs.text: Freeze-dried beef liver and organ capsules are taken as a convenient stand-in for eating organ meats, for skin, energy and general nutrition. They are marketed as a multivitamin alternative; no appearance trials exist.

bone-marrow-bone-broth.text: Bone broth and marrow are consumed for collagen, with users hoping for firmer skin and healthier joints. They are long-standing foods; no published trials examine appearance.

chain: Used in cooking and on skin
beef-tallow.text: Beef tallow is used in ancestral-diet cooking and increasingly applied to the face as a moisturiser. Its use as cooking fat is long-standing; its skin and appearance effects are untested in trials.

tallow-skincare.text: Users apply whipped tallow balms to the face as a moisturiser, preferring a simple animal-fat product to conventional creams. It is popular online, and published trials on tallow itself are lacking.

raw-honey-bee-pollen.text: Raw honey and bee pollen are promoted for skin and testosterone. Honey has some wound-care evidence; the appearance benefits of both are described as unproven.

fruitarian-diet.text: Some in looksmaxxing communities eat only fruit in pursuit of clean, glowing skin and a lean body. There are no appearance trials, and case reports focus on nutritional problems.

raw-vegan-diet.text: Followers eat uncooked plant foods hoping for better skin, leanness and general health. Small studies cover nutrition status, none cover looks, and B12 intake is a recurring topic.

vegan-diet.text: People adopt veganism for skin, leanness and, in anecdotal claims, lighter eye colour. Data are good for weight and cardiometabolic markers; appearance claims are mostly anecdotal.

chain: Less meat, more plants and fish
vegetarian-pescatarian.text: Vegetarian and pescatarian diets are used as reduced-meat options for skin, leanness and general health. Population data on health are decent; looks are not directly studied.

mediterranean-diet.text: The Mediterranean pattern is used as a well-researched baseline diet for general health, skin and weight control. Cardiovascular evidence is strong; appearance is not directly studied.

anti-inflammatory-diet.text: Users eat whole-food, low-processed diets to reduce facial puffiness and acne. Research targets inflammation markers and disease, not puffiness or acne directly.

dairy-free-for-skin.text: People avoid milk and sometimes other dairy to clear acne and, in some accounts, reduce facial puffiness. Observational studies link dairy to acne weakly; trials are lacking.

chain: Lower glycation and blood sugar swings
no-sugar-sugar-free-lifestyle.text: Users cut added sugar for clearer, younger-looking skin and a leaner body. Health guidelines support eating less sugar; skin-specific trials are thin.

gluten-free-for-skin.text: Some people go gluten-free hoping to clear acne or skin inflammation. It is essential for celiac-linked rashes; no acne trials were found for people without such conditions.

low-sodium-for-face-de-puffing.text: Users lower salt intake to reduce perceived facial water retention and look more defined. Low sodium lowers blood pressure, but facial effects are unstudied in these sources.
